item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is open to every paying developer at $2 / $10 until November 30: what to test before the price doubles
item.description: Google's strongest model left its cyber-only gate after two weeks, matched Argon's price for 19 days and published safety numbers that are worth reading more closely than the benchmark wins.
item.content:encoded:
Google's strongest model left its cyber-only gate after two weeks, matched Argon's price for 19 days and published safety numbers that are worth reading more closely than the benchmark wins.

Google made Gemini 4 Carbon generally available on November 10, thirteen days after releasing it to a selected group of cyber defenders in its Fairwind programme. Paying users can now call it through the Gemini API, AI Studio and Gemini for business, and it is wired into Android Studio, Gemini Enterprise, Antigravity and CodeMender. Google AI Ultra subscribers get it in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search and Antigravity. The cyber-tuned variant, "Carbon for cyber", stays behind Fairwind on a rolling basis.

The price and the deadline

Carbon is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, the same as Gemini 4 Argon. Google says the introductory period for both ends on November 30, after which they move to $4 and $20. That is the same step Google announced for Argon's launch pricing, now extended to Carbon, and it is the first time a frontier vendor has scheduled a price rise rather than a cut. For comparison, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is $2 / $10 with no announced change, Opus 5.5 is $4 / $20, OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol is $2 / $10, and GPT-5.6 Sol's own promotion ends the same day Google's does. From December 1 the mid-frontier tier will be $4 / $20 at two of the three big labs.

What Google is claiming

The announcement is built around agentic benchmarks rather than academic ones. Google says Carbon is first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR and Zapier's AutomationBench at more than twice the cost efficiency per task of the next external model, second on the Artificial Analysis Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark at more than six times lower average cost per task than the leader, and top of 23 configurations on Balyasny's financial intelligence suite. Artificial Analysis' own Intelligence Index puts Carbon at 59. Google's framing is careful: it says Argon "remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work" and Carbon is for long-horizon agents and security.

The numbers worth more attention are in the safety section. In simulated cyberattacks Google reports the per-attempt breach rate fell to 0.8% from Argon's 3.1%; on Gray Swan's attack-query set, success fell to 2.17% from 9.86%; external red-teaming by Trajectory Labs found no universal jailbreak in 132 hours and 13,000 requests; and on a 375-task agentic honesty benchmark Carbon passed 92% against Argon's 70%, declining to invent missing experimental data 98% of the time. Two weeks earlier Google reported a 0% success rate on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection test, with the caveat that robustness is still an area for improvement.

The counter-argument

Every figure above is Google's, on benchmarks Google chose, some of which are built by partners that also sell Carbon-powered products. Cost-per-task claims depend on token counts that reasoning models vary by effort setting, so "2x cheaper per task" can flip with a different budget. The cyber benchmarks that justify the gated variant are not public. And the honesty improvement, while large, is measured on a benchmark of Google's design; wait for METR, Artificial Analysis and the UK AISI to publish before updating a model policy.

Antigravity swarm

The developer-facing novelty is /swarm in Antigravity, in preview: a single prompt becomes a team of agents, with Carbon in the architect, coordinator and auditor roles and lighter models working in parallel isolated workspaces while adversarial verifiers test each change. Google's demos include a 906,000-triangle reconstruction of a railway platform from seven PDFs over ten overnight runs. It is the same orchestration pattern Anthropic and OpenAI have shipped in their coding tools, with Google's twist that the verifier is a separate adversarial agent.

What to do

Put Carbon and Argon on the same eval harness this week; the price parity makes the comparison free of budget politics for 19 days. Record token usage per task, not just pass rates, because that is what changes on December 1. If you use Gemini through Vertex rather than the Gemini API, check that pricing separately; Google's post covers the developer API. Pin model versions in config rather than aliases so the step-up cannot surprise a running agent. And if you are in Fairwind, the cyber variant's SEC-bench and ExploitGym leads are the ones to test against your own vulnerability queue.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 cuts the top tier to $8 / $40: what actually changes for buyers
item.description: Anthropic's flagship is 20% cheaper and, on its own numbers, far better at agentic coding, but the company still tells most customers to stay on Opus 5.5.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic's flagship is 20% cheaper and, on its own numbers, far better at agentic coding, but the company still tells most customers to stay on Opus 5.5.

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9 and, for the first time in the Mythos-class line, cut the price. Both list at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 / $50 for the 5.1 models launched in September. Cached input reads cost $0.20, batch requests are half price at $4 / $20, and a new fast mode that Anthropic says generates tokens up to 2.5 times faster costs double, $16 / $80.

What is new

Fable and Mythos remain one underlying model. Fable carries additional safeguards for cyber and biology tasks and is available to everyone on the Claude API, AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Mythos drops those safeguards and is reserved for organisations vetted through Anthropic's cyber and life-sciences verification programmes, though Claude Enterprise customers can use its vulnerability-detection capability through the Claude Security product without joining either.

On Anthropic's published tables, Fable 5.2 scores 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its highest effort setting, against 32.4% for Fable 5.1 and 45.5% for Opus 5.5. It posts 69.9% on FrontierSWE v2, 89.3% on OSWorld 2.1 and 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index, more than double 5.1's 17.9%. Anthropic also says outputs are up to 30% faster across effort levels and that at the default Medium effort the model finishes tasks with fewer tokens than 5.1 did.

The claim most relevant to buyers is a cost one: Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort roughly matches Opus 5.5 at Max on FrontierCode (45.3% versus 45.5%) at about half the cost per task. If that holds on your workload, the top tier stops being a luxury for a handful of jobs.

The counter-argument

Every number above is Anthropic's own, and several of the showcase results, including the 30-hour Lean formalisation of Fermat's Last Theorem by roughly 1,000 agents, were single runs. Gemini 4 Carbon still leads Anthropic's own table on AutomationBench and Chartography, and Opus 5.5 edges Fable 5.2 on the AA-Briefcase Elo (1800 versus 1785). Analysts quoted by InfoWorld made the point that matters for budgets: Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a task, and agentic work at higher effort levels can consume many more tokens than a single prompt did a year ago.

There is also a data-handling wrinkle. Customers eligible for zero data retention keep it with the new models through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards programme, which is still in private beta; everyone else accepts 30-day retention of prompts and outputs for safety monitoring. For regulated buyers that term can outweigh a 20% price cut, and procurement teams should get it in writing.

Where this leaves the price ladder

With this cut, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at $10 / $50 becomes the most expensive flagship in our pricing tracker, with GPT-6 Cyber at $20 / $100 above it as a gated special case. The mid-tier is now crowded at $2 / $10 (Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon until November 30) and the budget tier sits at $0.10 / $0.50 (Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna and, as of this week, Meta's Muse Ember). Anthropic's own recommendation is unchanged: Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, Fable or Mythos for the hardest open-ended tasks.

What to do

Pick three workloads where Opus 5.5 currently fails or needs heavy human review and run them on Fable 5.2 at High effort, measuring cost per completed task rather than per token. Check whether your account is eligible for zero data retention before routing anything sensitive. If you are on Fable 5.1, note that it still lists at $10 / $50; the saving only arrives when you change the model ID to claude-fable-5-2. And wait for independent evaluations, which usually arrive within a week of a release of this size, before making the switch permanent.

item.title: Inkling 2 Small: a 594B-parameter model trained in 68 hours, priced at $0.30 per million tokens
item.description: Thinking Machines' second-generation model is a case study in how cheap sparse pretraining has become, and a direct price attack on the mid-tier where closed labs earn their API revenue.
item.content:encoded:
Thinking Machines' second-generation model is a case study in how cheap sparse pretraining has become, and a direct price attack on the mid-tier where closed labs earn their API revenue.

Thinking Machines Lab, the company Mira Murati founded in 2025, released Inkling 2 Small on November 5. It is the first model of the lab's second generation and, on the company's own description, its most capable so far, with what it calls a big jump in agentic coding and vision.

The architecture is a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer: 594 billion total parameters, of which about 17 billion are active for any given token. Each token is routed to 8 of 384 experts across 48 layers, with a mix of local and global attention. The model accepts text and images and produces text, with a 1-million-token context window and variable effort settings.

The training recipe is the story

What makes the release notable for ML practitioners is how much the lab disclosed about cost. Pretraining ran on 8.4 trillion tokens in 68 hours on Nvidia GB300 NVL72 racks, using native NVFP4, a four-bit floating-point format, throughout. Reinforcement learning then ran for nine days on 2,048 GPUs: 1,075 steps and more than 17 million rollouts totalling over 3 trillion tokens, with coding making up 38.5% of rollouts and 65% of RL tokens. The median rollout lasted eight minutes; the 99th percentile ran four hours.

Those figures describe a frontier-adjacent model trained in well under two weeks of wall-clock time. They also show where the effort has moved. Pretraining is now the cheap part; the long-horizon RL phase, with hours-long agentic episodes, is where the compute and the engineering go.

Performance, honestly stated

The lab did not publish a standard benchmark table at launch, which is unusual and worth noting. It did say the model still trails OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol on its own alignment evaluations, and it listed limitations plainly: no audio, verbosity, imperfect tool selection in codebases with many skills, weaker performance on long multi-turn conversations and on under-represented languages. One demonstration had the model fine-tune a 4-billion-parameter Qwen model for time-series forecasting in a little over four hours and $426 of a $500 budget, cutting error by about 15% on unseen data. Third-party reports cite a strong result on SWE-Bench Pro Hard; we have not verified it against a primary source and leave it out of our tracker until the lab publishes it.

Pricing and availability

Inference is available now through Tinker, the company's fine-tuning and inference platform, at a listed $0.30 per million input tokens, $0.03 for cached input and $1.00 for output, according to a reading of Tinker's pricing page on November 7. For comparison, the cheapest closed mid-tier models in our pricing tracker are Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol at $2 / $10, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon at $2 / $10 until its launch pricing ends on November 30. Only OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, at $0.10 / $0.50, is cheaper, and it is positioned as a small model.

The weights are not yet public. The lab says it intends to publish them under Apache 2.0 in the weeks after launch, conditional on completed external safety testing and red-teaming, following the staged-release framework it published on July 31. That is a meaningful commitment: once weights are published they cannot be withdrawn, and gating the step on third-party testing rather than a calendar is a model other open-weight labs have not adopted.

The counter-argument

Sparse models with 17 billion active parameters are cheap to serve but have historically lagged dense frontier models on the hardest reasoning tasks, and the absence of a benchmark table makes it hard to know where this one lands. Tinker-only availability also means no self-hosting, no third-party inference providers and no enterprise agreements for now. Treat the price as a signal of where the market is heading rather than a number you can budget against today.

What to watch

The weights release and its licence terms, the first independent evaluations once the model is downloadable, and whether inference providers list it at or below Tinker's price. We have added Inkling 2 Small to both trackers and will update the pricing row from primary once the lab publishes an API rate card.
